verdict.rationale: The institution text Genesis 2:24 pairs the masculine word for man (ish, H0376) with the singular suffixed feminine word for his wife (ishto, from ishshah, H0802), uses the verbs leave (azab, H5800) and cleave (dabaq, H1692), and culminates in one flesh (basar echad), where the numeral one (echad, H0259) is the plain numeral one modifying flesh (basar, H1320). Genesis 1:27 supplies the creation-account binary male (zakar) and female (neqebah) (H2145, H5347), translated in the Greek of Matthew 19:4 and Mark 10:6 as male (arsen) and female (thelys) (G0730, G2338). Jesus, speaking with the authority of the Lord, cites both texts together (Matthew 19:4-6, Mark 10:6-9), declares that the two (hoi dyo) (G1417) become into one flesh (eis sarka mian) (G4561 with the feminine numeral one (mian) from heis, G1520), names God as the agent with the verb yoked together (synezeuxen, from syzeugnymi, G4801, a verb that occurs only at Matthew 19:6 and Mark 10:9 in the entire New Testament canon), and prohibits separation (chorizo, G5563). Ephesians 5:31 reproduces Genesis 2:24 verbatim and applies it with reference to Christ and to the church (eis Christon kai eis ten ekklesian) (church = ekklesia, G1577). The same one (echad) of Genesis 2:24 is invoked in Malachi 2:15 of the wife-of-youth covenant (berith, H1285), and the qualifier of one wife a husband (mias gynaikos andra) (G1520, G1135, G0435), in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6 lexically (that is, in the actual words used) presupposes the same monogamous norm. The pair (the dyad), the singular numeral, the leave-and-cleave verbs, the divine joining verb, and the New Testament reuse converge.

scripture.reasoning: The creation account states that God created the human in his image, male (zakar, H2145) and female (neqebah, H5347) he created them. The two gendered nouns name the original creational pair, and the immediate context of Genesis 1:28 attaches the procreation mandate (the command to bear children) to that pair. This verse supplies the lexical source (the word-level basis) for the Greek male and female (arsen kai thelys) cited by Jesus in Matthew 19:4 and Mark 10:6.

The verse states that a man (ish, H0376) leaves (azab, H5800) his father and mother and cleaves (dabaq, H1692) to his wife (his wife = ishto, the suffixed singular form of ishshah, H0802), and they become one flesh (one flesh = basar echad, H1320 plus the numeral one = echad, H0259). The masculine man (ish) is paired with the feminine wife (ishshah) and the singular pronominal suffix (the singular 'his' attached to the noun), the numeral one (echad) quantifies the resulting flesh as one, and the verbs leave (azab) and cleave (dabaq) frame a permanent re-attachment that supersedes the prior parental bond.

Jesus appeals to the Creator who from the beginning (from the beginning = ap arches) made them male and female (arsen kai thelys) (G0730, G2338), citing Genesis 1:27 in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, or LXX). The appeal by the Lord locates the male and female pairing at the act of creation rather than at later custom and frames the answer to the divorce question by recourse to the original lexical definition (the original word-level meaning).

Jesus quotes Genesis 2:24 from the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, or LXX). A man will be joined (will be joined = kollethesetai, from kollao, G2853) to his wife (his wife = gynaiki, a singular dative form meaning 'to the wife'), and the two (hoi dyo) (G1417) will be into one flesh (eis sarka mian) (flesh = sarx, G4561, with the feminine numeral one = mian from heis, G1520). The explicit numeral two paired with one flesh quantifies the union as a pair fused into a single entity, and the word for wife (gynaiki) is grammatically singular.

The conclusion states they are no longer two (dyo) but one flesh (one flesh = mia sarx), and what God yoked together (yoked together = synezeuxen, a completed past action from the verb syzeugnymi, G4801) let no person separate (separate = chorizo, G5563). The yoking verb names God as the agent of the union, and the separating verb names the prohibited human act. The lexical store confirms G4801 occurs only twice in the entire New Testament canon, here and at Mark 10:9, marking yoke-together (syzeugnymi) as a near hapax (a word that occurs only once or very rarely in the entire Bible) tied uniquely to the marriage-pair pronouncement.

The Markan parallel records that from the beginning of creation (apo arches ktiseos) God made them male and female (arsen kai thelys) (G0730, G2338). The phrase from the beginning of creation (apo arches ktiseos) anchors the male and female pairing at the act of creation, reinforcing the Matthean appeal independently in a second Gospel witness.

A man (man = anthropos) leaves father and mother and is joined (is joined = proskollethesetai, from a strengthened compound form of join = kollao, G2853) to his wife (his wife = gynaika, a singular accusative form, that is, the wife as direct object), the Markan citation of Genesis 2:24 paralleling the Matthean leave-and-cleave structure with the wife as the singular feminine object of the joining.

The two (the two = hoi dyo, G1417) will be into one flesh (eis sarka mian), and so they are no longer two but one flesh (one flesh = mia sarx, G4561 with one = mian from heis, G1520). The numeral two against the singular one flesh repeats the pair-to-unity arithmetic of the Matthean parallel.

What God yoked together (yoked together = synezeuxen, G4801) let no person separate (separate = chorizo, G5563). The Markan conclusion matches Matthew word for word in naming God as the joining agent and prohibiting human separation, attesting the divine institution and intended permanence in a second witness and completing the only two New Testament occurrences of yoke-together (syzeugnymi).

Paul reproduces Genesis 2:24: a man leaves father and mother and is joined (is joined = proskollethesetai, from kollao, G2853) to his wife (his wife = gynaiki, singular), and the two (hoi dyo) (G1417) will be into one flesh (eis sarka mian) (G4561, G1520). The verbatim reuse of the creation text in an epistle (a New Testament letter) shows the one-flesh pair treated as the standing norm for marriage in apostolic instruction.

Paul calls this a great mystery (great mystery = mega mysterion) and states he speaks with reference to Christ and to the church (eis Christon kai eis ten ekklesian) (church = ekklesia, G1577). The clause but I speak (ego de lego) marks the prior verse as the base text and this verse as Paul's application, so the marriage one-flesh union supplies the figure for the Christ-and-church relation, which is the picturing clause of the proposition (the part of the question that says marriage pictures Christ and the church).

The prophet names the wife as the wife of your covenant (eshet beritheka, with covenant = berith, H1285), grounding the marriage bond in covenant language explicitly. This is the canonical source for the covenant term that does not appear in Genesis 2:24 itself, supplying via the principle of letting Scripture interpret Scripture (analogia scripturae) the covenant framing of the institution.

The verse states he did not make one (one = echad, H0259), and the immediate continuation calls for faithfulness to the wife of one's youth in the same context that names the marriage as covenant (berith). The reuse of the very numeral one (echad) from Genesis 2:24 in a polemic against marital unfaithfulness binds the institution text to a one-wife monogamy norm at the canonical level. The verse is grammatically difficult but its term one (echad) lexically echoes Genesis 2:24's one flesh (basar echad).

The verse describes the adulteress who has forsaken (forsaken = azab, H5800) the companion of her youth and forgotten the covenant of her God (covenant of her God = berith elohim, H1285). The same verb leave (azab) that in Genesis 2:24 names the leaving of father and mother in order to cleave to the wife is here inverted to describe the abandoning of the marriage covenant, lexically confirming that the marriage bond is itself a covenant (berith).

The overseer qualification reads literally a husband of one wife (mias gynaikos andra) (with G1520 'one' in the feminine genitive (the 'of-X' form) mias, G1135 'wife' in the genitive 'of a wife' gynaikos, G0435 'husband' in the accusative (direct-object form) andra). The numeral one (mias) attached to wife (gynaikos) attached to husband (andra) is a settled apostolic shorthand for the monogamous norm, since polygamy or serial divorce would render the phrase incoherent. The verse presupposes the one-man-one-woman pattern as the baseline for an exemplary household.

The elder qualification reads the husband of one wife (mias gynaikos aner) (G1520 'one' = mias, G1135 'wife' = gynaikos, G0435 'husband' = aner), reproducing the same construction as 1 Timothy 3:2 in a second pastoral epistle. The repetition across two letters confirms the construction is a fixed apostolic formula encoding the monogamous baseline.

Paul charges that a wife is not to be separated (separated = chorizo, G5563) from her husband, using the same verb Jesus used in the prohibition of Matthew 19:6 and Mark 10:9. The apostolic reuse of the Lord's own vocabulary ports the divine joining and the prohibition of separation forward into Pauline marriage ethics, with the verb to marry (gameo, G1060) supplying the standard marrying verb in the surrounding context.

complicating_texts.resolution: The verse is the foundational text and not against the proposition, but the word covenant (berith, H1285) does not appear in it. The covenant framing rests on later texts. Malachi 2:14 names the wife as the wife of your covenant (eshet beritheka), and Proverbs 2:17 calls the marriage bond the covenant of her God (berith elohim). The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge (TSK) cross-references invoke both, so the covenant element is lexically supported elsewhere even though it is not stated in the institution text itself.

The clause the mystery is great (mega to mysterion estin) could be read as making the mystery primary and the marriage secondary, which would weaken marriage as the literal referent. The grammar resolves this. Paul says but I speak (ego de lego), with reference to Christ and to the church (eis Christon kai eis ten ekklesian), indicating that he is applying the just-quoted Genesis 2:24 marriage text figuratively to Christ and the church. The marriage one-flesh union remains the base sense and the Christ-and-church relation is the figure drawn from it, which is the picturing claim in the proposition.

Lamech in the Cainite line takes for himself two wives (two wives = shtey nashim, with H8147 'two' = shenayim, and the plural of H0802 'woman' = ishshah), the first polygamous union in the canon. The narrative reports this as the act of Lamech without commendation, situated within the violence and arrogance of Genesis 4:23-24. The genre is historical narrative, not prescription (not commanding it as a rule), and the use of the dual plural 'wives' (nashim) against the singular 'his wife' (ishto) of Genesis 2:24 is a lexical deviation marked by the descent of Cain. The patriarchal polygamy that follows (Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon) is likewise narrated descriptively and shown to produce strife in every case (Sarah and Hagar, Leah and Rachel, the succession crisis of 2 Samuel), without ever recasting the Genesis 2:24 lexical norm.

The Mosaic instruction to the king is he shall not multiply for himself wives (lo yarbeh lo nashim) (H7235A 'multiply' = rabah, with the negative H3808 'not' = lo and the plural 'wives' = nashim from H0802 ishshah). The prohibition presupposes the legitimate norm is not multiplication, lexically aligning with the singular 'his wife' (ishto) of Genesis 2:24 against the royal polygamy reported in 1 Kings 11.

The case law begins if a man has two wives (ki tihyenah le-ish shtey nashim) (H8147 'two' = shenayim, plural of 'woman' = ishshah). The construction is regulative (laying down a rule for a case that exists), not endorsing, addressing inheritance for a son born to a hated wife in an existing polygamous arrangement. The verb is the if-then clause (a conditional) if it happens (ki tihyenah), signaling that the law contemplates a situation that occurs rather than commanding it. Jesus in Matthew 19:8 applies the same hermeneutic (interpretive method) to the divorce certificate of Deuteronomy 24:1, calling it a concession with the words from the beginning it was not so (ap arches de ou gegonen houtos).

Jesus distinguishes Moses' permission of divorce (he permitted = epetrepsen, G2010) on account of hardness of heart (hardness of heart = sklerokardia) from the original creation pattern (from the beginning it was not so = ap arches de ou gegonen houtos). The lexical signal is that from the beginning (ap arches) outranks the later concession, so the Old Testament regulatory texts on polygamy and divorce certificates are accommodations to fallen practice rather than redefinitions of the institution. This is the canon's own hermeneutic (interpretive method) for reading the patriarchal polygamy narratives.

variants.note: No variant units were supplied in the bundle for the cited Gospel and epistle verses. The marked apparatus sigla (the symbols flagging textual variants) in the SBLGNT surface forms (for example around 'the father' = ton patera and 'the wife' = ten gynaiki in Ephesians 5:31, and the leave-and-cleave clause word order at Mark 10:7) touch word order and the presence of clauses but do not alter the male and female pairing, the numeral two, the one flesh, the divine joining verb, or the Christ-and-church application. The hapax (a word that occurs only once or very rarely in the entire Bible) distribution of G4801 yoke-together (syzeugnymi), attested only at Matthew 19:6 and Mark 10:9, holds across the major manuscript witnesses. The Genesis, Malachi, and Proverbs anchors are outside the scope of the critical edition of New Testament textual variants (the ECM apparatus). The verdict holds across the readings available.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 as a creation ordinance (a standing rule instituted at creation), the male and female pairing and the one-flesh union are instituted at the beginning and carried forward as binding for all subsequent marriage, which Jesus confirms by appealing from the beginning (ap arches) and from the beginning of creation (apo arches ktiseos).

The covenant label for marriage is lexically grounded in Malachi 2:14 wife of your covenant (eshet beritheka) and Proverbs 2:17 covenant of her God (berith elohim). The institution text Genesis 2:24 supplies the pair and the one-flesh union, and the prophetic and wisdom corpus supplies the covenant term, so the covenant union framing is supported by the principle of letting Scripture interpret Scripture (analogia scripturae) across the canon even though it is not derivable from the institution text alone.

Reading Ephesians 5:31-32 as typology (where an earlier reality prefigures a later one), the one-flesh marriage union foreshadows the union of Christ and the church (church = ekklesia, G1577), so the picturing clause of the proposition is the load-bearing application Paul makes of the creation text, marked by but I speak with reference to Christ and to the church (ego de lego eis Christon kai eis ten ekklesian).

Reading the patriarchal narratives of Lamech in Genesis 4:19, Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon as a complicating canon witness, the polygamous unions are reported in narrative genre and consistently linked to strife and prohibition (Deuteronomy 17:17 against royal multiplication, the deuteronomic regulation in Deuteronomy 21:15-17, the strife of the matriarchs). On its strongest lexical form, the Old Testament pattern is descriptive accommodation, not prescription (not commanding it as a rule), and Jesus' from the beginning (ap arches) in Matthew 19:4-8 explicitly subordinates such later allowances to the original institution. The reading complicates rather than overturns the creational pair.

On the strongest reading of Matthew 19:6 and Mark 10:9, the divine yoking (yoked together = synezeuxen) and the prohibition of separation (separate = chorizo) imply lexical permanence with no licit dissolution. The Matthew 5:32 and 19:9 sexual immorality (porneia) clauses and Paul's 1 Corinthians 7:15 not enslaved (ou dedoulotai) qualify the strictness for specific cases without reopening the pair itself. The intended-for-life clause of the proposition is lexically supported in its core, with the qualifications recorded in the canon itself.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on grammatico-historical reading (reading the text by its grammar and historical setting) of the gendered nouns, the numerals one and two, the joining verbs yoke-together (syzeugnymi) and join (kollao), and the prohibition verb separate (chorizo), supported by the principle of letting Scripture interpret Scripture (analogia scripturae) linking Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 to Malachi 2:14-15, Proverbs 2:17, Matthew 19:4-9, Mark 10:6-9, Ephesians 5:31-32, 1 Timothy 3:2, Titus 1:6, and 1 Corinthians 7:10-11, and by progressive revelation (the truth being more fully disclosed over the course of the Bible) in that the Christ-and-church application is disclosed in Ephesians 5:32. The citation by the Lord of the creation texts is the lexical engine of the verdict.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Examine what the lexical data (word-level evidence) of Genesis 1:27, Genesis 2:24, Matthew 19:4-6, Mark 10:6-9, and Ephesians 5:31-32 indicate about the parties to marriage, its duration, its origin, and any figurative use, without presupposing the terms covenant or picturing Christ and the church.
stem_audit.notes: The stem loads three interpretive terms ahead of the data. Covenant union imports a covenant category that Genesis 2:24 does not state, though Malachi 2:14 and Proverbs 2:17 supply it elsewhere. Intended for life states a permanence conclusion that must be tested against the verbs yoked together (synezeuxen) and separate (chorizo) rather than assumed. Picturing Christ and the church states the Ephesians 5:32 typology (the earlier-reality-prefiguring-a-later-one reading) as settled. The verdict was derived on the original stem, but each loaded term was checked against the lexical evidence and each is supported: the pair and one flesh and divine joining directly in the anchors, the covenant term by cross-reference to Malachi 2:14 and Proverbs 2:17, the permanence by the verbs yoked together (synezeuxen) and separate (chorizo) together with the sexual immorality (porneia) and not enslaved (ou dedoulotai) qualifications in Matthew 5:32, Matthew 19:9, and 1 Corinthians 7:15, and the typology by Ephesians 5:32. No verdict change from prior. Affirms remains true at high confidence.

lay_summary: The original-language words behind these verses point in one direction. In Genesis 1:27 God makes the human male and female, that is, male (zakar) and female (neqebah), and in Genesis 2:24 the Hebrew pairs a masculine word for man (ish) with a singular feminine word for his wife (ishshah) and says the two become one flesh (basar echad), where one (echad) is the plain numeral one. A man leaves father and mother and cleaves to his wife, using the verbs leave (azab) and cleave (dabaq) that describe a permanent re-attachment. When Jesus is asked about marriage in Matthew 19 and Mark 10, he goes back to the beginning of creation and quotes both texts together. The Greek translates the binary as male (arsen) and female (thelys), and the union as the two into one flesh (hoi dyo eis sarka mian). He adds that God himself yoked them together with the verb yoke-together (synezeuxen), a word that appears in the entire New Testament only here and in the Markan parallel, and forbids any person to separate them with the verb separate (chorizo). Paul in Ephesians 5:31 repeats the same Genesis 2:24 quotation word for word, then says in verse 32 that he is speaking with reference to Christ and the church (ekklesia), treating the marriage union as a picture of that larger relation. The same numeral one (echad) of Genesis 2:24 turns up again in Malachi 2:15 against marital unfaithfulness, where the wife is called the wife of your covenant (berith), and Proverbs 2:17 calls the bond the covenant of her God. The apostolic qualification for overseers and elders in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6 reads literally a husband of one wife (mias gynaikos andra), presupposing the same monogamous pattern. Paul reuses the Lord's verb separate (chorizo) in 1 Corinthians 7:10 for the same prohibition. The Old Testament also reports patriarchal polygamy starting with Lamech in Genesis 4:19, but in narrative genre tied to strife and explicitly limited by Deuteronomy 17:17 and by Jesus' own from the beginning (ap arches) argument in Matthew 19:8, which treats later allowances as concessions, not redefinitions. The words, the numerals, the joining and separating verbs, and the apostolic reuse converge on a one-man-and-one-woman union, set up by God at creation, meant to last, and used as a figure of Christ and the church.
